doctrine:
**Reiterated:** the reliability of an out-of-court identification is tested by the **totality of circumstances**: (1) the witness's opportunity to view the criminal at the time of the crime; (2) the witness's degree of attention at that time; (3) the accuracy of any prior description given by the witness; (4) the length of time between the crime and the identification; (5) the level of certainty demonstrated by the witness at the identification; and (6) the suggestiveness of the identification procedure. The Court also listed the twelve "danger signals" that tend to show an out-of-court identification may be erroneous (from *People v. Jimenez*). **A photographic identification is not suggestive where the victim was shown photographs of different men every day, the accused was not singled out, and the victim immediately recognized him when she saw his photograph.** A two-month gap does not defeat the identification where the victim saw the assailant's face up close, including by the light of his flashlight, and was not distracted.

There is no standard reaction of a rape victim; failure to shout or call for help does not impair her credibility. "Lust is no respecter of time or place": rape is not always committed in seclusion. The trial court's assessment of credibility is respected on appeal unless significant matters were overlooked, and it carries greater weight when affirmed by the CA (all reiterated).

Rape under **Article 266-A(1)(a) of the RPC**, as amended by RA 8353, requires (1) carnal knowledge of the victim, (2) accomplished through force, threat, or intimidation. A knife held to the victim's nape with a threat to hurt her if she screamed, followed by punches when she resisted, establishes force, threat, or intimidation. The penalty is reclusion perpetua (Art. 266-B), with PHP 75,000 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages, plus 6% annual interest from finality until full payment.
facts:
Accused-appellant Ronaldo Infortuno, Sr. was charged with forcible abduction with rape of 17-year-old AAA, a distant neighbor in San Ildefonso, Bulacan. According to the prosecution, at around 1:00 to 1:30 a.m. on July 22, 2017, a man entered the room where AAA was sleeping with her younger brother. He poked a knife at her nape and whispered, "Subukan mong sumigaw. Masasaktan ka." He tied her hands, gagged her, and brought her to a rice field. There he cut her shirt and bra with scissors and removed her pajama and panty. When she resisted his first attempt at penetration, he punched her stomach and right thigh. He moved her to another place and had carnal knowledge of her. Afterwards he made her lie down and, using a small flashlight, cut her pubic hair. AAA saw his face by the light of the flashlight. He then let her go.

AAA immediately told her grandmother, other relatives and her mother, MMM, and they reported the incident to the police. The assailant was a stranger to AAA, so his identity was unknown; she told her mother that she did not know his name but would recognize his face. Every day MMM showed AAA pictures of different people. Learning from neighbors that a drinking session had been held across the highway that night, MMM mentioned several names, which AAA did not recognize. One of them was the accused, who was working on the house next door. MMM found his photographs on Facebook. On October 2, 2017, about two months after the rape, MMM showed them to AAA, who immediately said, "Siya, siya ang naggahasa sa akin." A medico-legal officer found injuries and "clear evidence of recent blunt penetrating trauma to the hymen."

The accused denied the charge and said he was at a drinking session in another barangay from about 7:00 p.m. until about 6:00 a.m. The RTC of Malolos City (Branch 18, November 4, 2020) convicted him of forcible abduction with rape and imposed reclusion perpetua and damages. On appeal, he attacked AAA's credibility and identification. He argued that it was dark, the flashlight pointed at her private part and not at his face, she had never met him, she gave no prior description, and she identified him only two months later after her mother showed her his photograph. He also argued that a criminal would not use a flashlight, that force was not proved because she did not see the knife and did not shout, and that forcible abduction is absorbed in rape. The CA (March 27, 2023, CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 15216) affirmed with modification, convicting him of rape under Article 266-A(1) instead of forcible abduction with rape, with the same penalty and damages.
issues: Whether the CA erred in finding accused-appellant guilty beyond reasonable doubt of rape, including whether AAA was a credible witness and whether her out-of-court identification of accused-appellant was reliable.
ruling:
**1. No. The conviction for rape was affirmed.**

*Credibility.* The Court held that not all rape victims react the same way: "some may shout, some may faint, and some may be shocked into insensibility." AAA's failure to call for help therefore did not affect her credibility. The argument that crimes are usually committed clandestinely also failed, because lust is no respecter of time or place. The trial court, affirmed by the CA, gave full credence to AAA, and no significant matter was overlooked.

*Identification.* Applying the totality of circumstances test and the danger signals, the Court found AAA's identification credible. Although there were no lights in the house or the rice field, AAA saw the accused's face when he placed the flashlight in her mouth. The light pointed toward her private part, but he was in the same direction, so she could see his face, and she was not distracted. AAA also testified that his face was "lapit na lapit" when he grabbed her and held the knife to her. **On the two-month gap, the Court found the photographic procedure "not at all suggestive": MMM showed AAA photographs of different men every day, nothing showed the accused was singled out, and AAA immediately recognized him only when she saw his photograph on October 2, 2017.**

*Elements.* AAA's testimony, corroborated by the medico-legal findings, proved carnal knowledge. Force, threat, or intimidation was clear: the accused held a knife to AAA's nape and threatened to hurt her if she screamed, cut her clothes with scissors, and punched her when she resisted. Reclusion perpetua was correctly imposed under Article 266-B, and the PHP 75,000 awards of civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages were affirmed, with 6% legal interest per annum from finality.
disposition: The appeal was DISMISSED. The CA's March 27, 2023 Decision in CA-G.R. CR-HC No. 15216 was AFFIRMED. Infortuno was found GUILTY beyond reasonable doubt of rape and sentenced to reclusion perpetua. He was ordered to pay AAA PHP 75,000.00 as civil indemnity, PHP 75,000.00 as moral damages and PHP 75,000.00 as exemplary damages, all with 6% legal interest per annum from finality of the Decision until full payment.

bar_questions.q: Past midnight, a stranger entered the room of BBB, 19, held a knife to her neck, dragged her to a vacant lot and raped her. The lot was dark, but the assailant's face was inches from hers, and he later switched on a penlight to look for his belongings, lighting up his face. BBB reported the rape that morning but said she did not know the man's name, only that she would know his face. For six weeks her brother showed her photographs of different men from social media every day; she recognized none. When she was shown the photographs of Dario, a worker at a nearby construction site, she immediately said, "Siya po iyon." At trial, Dario argues that the out-of-court identification is unreliable because of the darkness, the six-week delay, and the use of photographs. Is Dario correct?

alac.answer: No. BBB's out-of-court identification passes the totality of circumstances test and is credible.
alac.legal_basis: The reliability of an out-of-court identification is determined by the totality of circumstances test: (1) the witness's opportunity to view the criminal at the time of the crime; (2) the witness's degree of attention; (3) the accuracy of any prior description; (4) the length of time between the crime and the identification; (5) the level of certainty at the identification; and (6) the suggestiveness of the procedure. In People v. Infortuno (G.R. No. 269722, January 6, 2026), the Court upheld a rape victim's identification of the accused from a Facebook photograph about two months after the crime. The victim saw his face by the light of his flashlight, she was shown photographs of different men daily, the accused was not singled out, and she immediately recognized him.
alac.application: BBB had a close view of the assailant, whose face was inches from hers and later lit by the penlight, and nothing distracted her attention. From the start she said she would recognize his face. Six weeks is not so long as to make the identification doubtful. The procedure was not suggestive: she was shown many different men daily, recognized none of them, and immediately and positively identified Dario when she saw his photographs. Darkness alone does not defeat an identification made under these circumstances.
alac.conclusion: Dario's objection fails because BBB's photographic identification of him is reliable under the totality of circumstances test.

bar_questions.q: CCC was raped at night by a man she had never seen before. At the police station that morning, she told the investigator that it was too dark and she could not identify her attacker. Five months later, a police officer showed her one photograph, that of Efren, saying, "This is the man the neighbors suspect. Is this him?" CCC said yes. No other photograph or lineup was shown to her. Would CCC's out-of-court identification satisfy the totality of circumstances test? Explain.

alac.answer: No. The identification is doubtful because the procedure was suggestive and several danger signals are present.
alac.legal_basis: Under the totality of circumstances test, the court considers, among others, the witness's opportunity to view the criminal, the length of time between the crime and the identification, and the suggestiveness of the identification procedure. Danger signals that an out-of-court identification may be erroneous include: the witness originally stated that she could not identify anyone; before the crime, the witness had limited opportunity to see the accused; and a considerable time elapsed between the witness's view of the criminal and the identification. (People v. Infortuno, G.R. No. 269722, January 6, 2026, citing People v. Jimenez)
alac.application: In Infortuno, the Court upheld the identification because the victim saw the assailant's face by flashlight, said from the start that she would recognize him, and picked him out of photographs of different men shown to her daily, without his being singled out. Here, every one of those safeguards is missing. CCC said at the outset that she could not identify her attacker. She had never seen him before. Five months passed. She was shown a single photograph accompanied by a remark that he was the suspect, which singled Efren out and suggested the answer.
alac.conclusion: CCC's out-of-court identification would not pass the totality of circumstances test and cannot by itself establish Efren's identity as the rapist beyond reasonable doubt.

bar_questions.q: Felix poked a knife at the nape of DDD while she slept and whispered that she would be hurt if she screamed. He tied her hands and brought her to a field, where he punched her when she resisted and then had carnal knowledge of her. DDD admitted on cross-examination that she never actually saw the knife and that she never shouted for help. (a) Was the element of force, threat, or intimidation proved, and does her failure to shout impair her credibility? (b) If Felix is convicted of rape, what civil liabilities should be imposed?

alac.answer: (a) Yes, force, threat, or intimidation was proved, and her failure to shout does not impair her credibility. (b) Felix should pay civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages of PHP 75,000.00 each, with 6% legal interest per annum from finality of the judgment until full payment.
alac.legal_basis: Under Article 266-A(1)(a) of the Revised Penal Code, as amended by RA 8353, rape is committed by a man who has carnal knowledge of a woman through force, threat, or intimidation. There is no standard form of reaction for a victim of sexual assault; failure to call for help does not impair the credibility of a rape victim. In People v. Infortuno (G.R. No. 269722, January 6, 2026), the Court found force, threat, or intimidation where the accused held a knife to the victim's nape, threatened to hurt her if she screamed, and punched her when she resisted. It imposed reclusion perpetua and awarded PHP 75,000.00 each as civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages, all with 6% interest per annum from finality.
alac.application: (a) Felix's threat that DDD would be hurt if she screamed, made while pressing a knife to her nape, is intimidation whether or not she saw the blade. Tying her hands and punching her when she resisted is force. DDD's silence is consistent with fear and does not make her testimony less believable. (b) Following Infortuno, a conviction for simple rape carries civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages of PHP 75,000.00 each, earning 6% interest per annum from finality.
alac.conclusion: Felix may be convicted of rape through force, threat, or intimidation and held liable for PHP 75,000.00 each in civil indemnity, moral damages and exemplary damages, with 6% annual interest from finality.

notes: The Information charged forcible abduction with rape; the CA convicted for rape only, and the Supreme Court affirmed without separately discussing why forcible abduction was not imposed. The narration says AAA and her family reported the incident to the police on the day of the crime, while AAA testified that she lodged her complaint on October 2, 2017, when she saw the accused's photograph. The decision mentions an act of oral sex during the incident but does not treat it as a separate offense; it was not charged. Bar Q2 applies the Court's danger signals to facts the Court did not decide; its answer is derived from the test as the Court stated it.
